title: Refactoring Techniques
tagline: Improve code structure without changing observable behaviour — detect smells, apply named refactorings, and keep the test suite green the entire time.

sections.content:
**Refactoring** is the disciplined process of improving the internal structure of existing code without altering its external behaviour. It is not rewriting — it is a sequence of small, named, behaviour-preserving transformations each verified by tests.

The concept was systematised by Martin Fowler in *Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code* (1999, 2nd ed. 2018), which catalogues over 60 named refactorings. The workflow is always the same: **red → green → refactor**. First, write a test that pins the current behaviour (or rely on existing tests). Then make the smallest meaningful structural improvement. Then run the tests to confirm nothing broke. Repeat. This is how large, frightening codebases are safely improved — one micro-step at a time.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    SMELL["Detect Code Smell\n(duplication, long method, etc.)"]
    TEST["Ensure Tests Cover\nthe Behaviour"]
    PICK["Pick Named Refactoring\n(Extract Function, etc.)"]
    APPLY["Apply Transformation"]
    GREEN["Run Tests — All Green?"]
    DONE["Commit Small Change"]
    FIX["Fix Broken Test or\nUndo Transformation"]
    SMELL --> TEST
    TEST --> PICK
    PICK --> APPLY
    APPLY --> GREEN
    GREEN -->|"yes"| DONE
    GREEN -->|"no"| FIX
    FIX --> APPLY
    DONE --> SMELL
sections.caption: Refactoring is a tight loop: smell → test → transform → verify. Each cycle is small enough to undo in seconds if tests break.

sections.title: Renovating a House Without Evicting the Tenants
sections.content:
Refactoring is like renovating a house while the tenants are still living in it. You can repaint a room (rename a variable), move a wall (extract a function), or rewire an outlet (change a data structure) — but the tenants must be able to use every door and every light switch throughout the process. The **tests are the tenants**: if any test fails, a door is broken and you must fix it before continuing.

A **code smell** is a sign the house needs work — not that it is about to collapse. A 200-line function is like a room that has accumulated furniture for a decade: it still works, but it is hard to clean and you cannot find anything. **Extract Function** is moving some of that furniture into a proper room. **Rename Variable** is replacing a mystery box labelled 'stuff' with a labelled container. The house still functions throughout; it just becomes progressively easier to live in.

**Code Smells** are surface symptoms suggesting a deeper design problem. Common smells include:

- **Long Method**: a function longer than ~20 lines is doing too much — extract sub-functions.
- **Duplicate Code**: the same logic in multiple places — extract to a shared function.
- **Large Class**: a class with too many responsibilities — split into focused classes (SRP).
- **Long Parameter List**: more than 3–4 parameters — introduce a Parameter Object.
- **Magic Numbers / Strings**: literal values without names — extract to named constants.
- **Dead Code**: unreachable or unused code — delete it; version control remembers it.
- **Feature Envy**: a method that uses another class's data more than its own — move it to that class.
- **Comments as Deodorant**: a comment explaining *what* code does is a hint the code should explain itself via better naming.

**Core Named Refactorings:**

- **Extract Function**: pull a block of code into its own named function. Inverse: *Inline Function*.
- **Rename Variable/Function/Class**: change a name to better communicate intent. The most important refactoring.
- **Introduce Parameter Object**: replace a cluster of related parameters with a single object.
- **Replace Magic Number with Symbolic Constant**: `const MAX_RETRIES = 3` instead of the literal `3`.
- **Extract Variable**: give a complex expression a name (`const isEligible = age >= 18 && !isBanned`).
- **Move Function**: relocate a function to the class/module where it logically belongs (Feature Envy fix).
- **Decompose Conditional**: extract complex `if/else` conditions and branches into named functions.
- **Replace Conditional with Polymorphism**: swap a long `switch` on type with a class hierarchy or strategy map.
- **Encapsulate Field**: expose a field only through accessor functions so you can add validation later.

**The test safety net** is non-negotiable. Refactoring *without* tests is just editing with hope. Even a basic test that calls the function and asserts its return value gives you the confidence to rename or restructure without fear.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    BEFORE["Before: long function
with magic numbers
and duplicated logic"]
    EF["Extract Function
(sub-steps become named fns)"]
    RV["Rename Variables
(intent made explicit)"]
    RC["Replace Magic Numbers
(named constants)"]
    DD["Deduplicate
(shared helper)"]
    AFTER["After: short focused functions
self-documenting names
zero duplication"]
    BEFORE --> EF --> RV --> RC --> DD --> AFTER
sections.caption: Each named refactoring is one small step. Chaining them transforms unreadable code into clean code without ever breaking the tests.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: Each transformation is a named refactoring: Extract Function (`isEligibleForDiscount`, `calcDiscount`), Rename (`process` → `calcFinalBalance`, `u`/`t`/`x` → descriptive names), Replace Magic Number (constants). The strategy map replaces a chain of `if`s with a data structure — adding a new type requires zero logic changes.

sections.label: Concept
sections.explanation: Introduce Parameter Object makes call-sites self-documenting and easy to extend. Extract Variable gives complex conditions meaningful names. Encapsulate Field is one of the most impactful refactorings for long-term correctness — it is the only way to add validation to a field without a massive search-and-replace.

sections.content: **Never refactor and add features at the same time.** Keep two separate commits: one pure refactoring (zero behaviour change, tests unchanged), and one feature addition. This way, if a bug is introduced, you know immediately which commit caused it. The discipline of keeping 'structural' and 'behavioural' changes separate is what makes refactoring safe in a team.

items: **Refactoring** is behaviour-preserving restructuring — the external contract stays identical; only the internal structure improves.
**Code smells** (long method, duplication, magic numbers, dead code) are signals, not crimes — they guide where to refactor next.
**Named refactorings** (Extract Function, Rename, Introduce Parameter Object, Encapsulate Field) are vocabulary: use the names when code-reviewing so teammates know exactly what changed and why.
**Tests are the safety net** — refactor only code covered by tests, and run them after every micro-step so regressions are caught immediately.
**Commit refactoring and feature work separately** so blame, bisect, and reverting remain clean and reliable.

quiz.question: What is the defining constraint of refactoring?
options: You must add at least one new test per refactoring session
The external observable behaviour must remain unchanged
You must use an IDE refactoring tool — manual edits don't count
Each refactoring must reduce the line count by at least 10%
quiz.explanation: Refactoring is specifically defined as improving internal structure WITHOUT changing external behaviour. If behaviour changes, it is a feature addition or bug fix, not a refactoring.

quiz.question: Which refactoring technique is being applied when you move a block of code into its own named function?
options: Rename Variable
Introduce Parameter Object
Extract Function
Encapsulate Field
quiz.explanation: Extract Function takes a code fragment and moves it into a new function with a name that communicates its purpose. It is the most frequently applied refactoring and the fix for the Long Method smell.

quiz.question: A function uses `0.1` and `1000` as literals throughout its body. Which refactoring should you apply?
options: Extract Function
Decompose Conditional
Replace Magic Number with Symbolic Constant
Move Function
quiz.explanation: Magic numbers are a code smell. Replace Magic Number with Symbolic Constant extracts the literal into a named constant (`const PREMIUM_DISCOUNT_RATE = 0.1`) so the intent is explicit and the value lives in one place.

quiz.question: What is a 'code smell'?
options: A runtime exception caused by poor error handling
A security vulnerability identified by a static analyser
A surface symptom in code that suggests a potential design problem worth investigating
An ESLint rule violation that must be fixed before committing
quiz.explanation: A code smell is an indicator — not a guarantee — that something may be worth refactoring. Long methods, duplicate code, and magic numbers are smells that guide you toward areas needing structural improvement.

quiz.question: You replace a chain of `if (type === 'express') ... else if (type === 'standard')...` checks with a lookup table `{ express: 25, standard: 10 }`. Which refactoring is this closest to?
options: Introduce Parameter Object
Extract Variable
Encapsulate Field
Replace Conditional with Polymorphism / Strategy
quiz.explanation: Replacing a type-checking conditional chain with a strategy map (or polymorphic dispatch) is the Replace Conditional with Polymorphism refactoring. It makes adding new cases a data change, not a logic change.

quiz.question: A method in `OrderService` reads and operates heavily on `Customer`'s internal data. What smell does this indicate, and what is the fix?
options: Dead Code — delete the method
Feature Envy — move the method to `Customer` where the data lives
Long Parameter List — introduce a Parameter Object
Large Class — split `OrderService` into two classes
quiz.explanation: Feature Envy is when a method is more interested in another class's data than its own. The fix is Move Function — relocate the method to the class whose data it uses, so the method and data live together.

quiz.question: Why should refactoring commits be kept separate from feature-addition commits?
options: Git cannot handle both types of change in the same commit
Mixing them makes it impossible to isolate which commit introduced a behaviour change or bug
Refactoring commits must be tagged with a version bump
IDEs require separate commits for refactoring to update their indexes
quiz.explanation: When a bug appears, `git bisect` and `git blame` are far more effective if every commit is either a pure structural change OR a behaviour change — never both. Mixing them makes causality hard to trace.

quiz.question: Which smell does a comment that explains *what* a block of code does (rather than *why*) typically indicate?
options: Dead Code — the code is no longer needed
Large Class — the class is too complex to understand without comments
The code should be clearer — use Extract Function and better names so the comment is unnecessary
Magic Numbers — literals need renaming
quiz.explanation: Martin Fowler calls this 'comments as deodorant': a comment explaining *what* code does signals the code should express that intent itself — via a well-named Extract Function or Extract Variable. Comments on *why* (business rules, non-obvious decisions) remain valuable.

quiz.question: Encapsulate Field replaces direct public field access with getter/setter methods. What key benefit does this provide?
options: It makes the field private so tests cannot access it
It reduces memory usage by removing the field
It creates a single place to add validation, logging, or derived logic without changing all callers
It automatically generates API documentation for the field
quiz.explanation: Once access is channelled through a setter, you can add validation (e.g. reject negative balances), logging, or notifications in one place. Without encapsulation, every direct write must be found and updated individually.

quiz.question: What is the Introduce Parameter Object refactoring, and why is it useful?
options: It wraps a return value in an object so multiple values can be returned
It groups related parameters into a single object, reducing Long Parameter List smell and making call-sites self-documenting
It converts an object parameter back into individual positional arguments for performance
It replaces all parameters with a global configuration object
quiz.explanation: When a function takes 5+ parameters, group related ones into a named object. This removes the Long Parameter List smell, makes call-sites self-documenting (named keys), and makes it easy to add optional fields without changing every caller.
